## Why Decode?

::: {.image-text-slide}

::: {.text-panel}
- ERPs: *does the group respond differently?*
- Decoding: *can we tell conditions apart in **this person's** EEG?*
- Individual read-out: biomarkers, speech BCIs
- Adults: ~70% binary accuracy
- Infant / developmental: lower
:::

::: {.image-panel}
![](figures/decoding/fig-schematic.svg){fig-alt="Schematic: single EEG trials become feature vectors; a classifier trained on some trials predicts the condition of held-out trials."}
:::

:::

::: {.takeaway}
Condition decoding is a feasibility test, not yet a measure of language ability.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:00 (cumulative 1:20). Group ERPs tell us about averages. Decoding asks whether one person's EEG carries enough information to tell two conditions apart, which is what any individual-level or BCI use would need. Adult binary decoding reaches about 70%; infant and developmental studies report less.
[Sources]
- LISTEN papers/Gatlinburg-2026.md (abstract): motivation, Bayet et al. 2020, Grootswagers et al. 2017, Gwilliams et al. 2022.
[/Sources]
:::

## The Feasibility Question

::: {.three-part-slide}
- **Who**<br>
  Adolescents: typically developing, verbal ASD, minimally verbal ASD, Angelman syndrome
- **What**<br>
  Within-person decoding of standard vs deviant **pure tones** (oddball, 480 / 120)
- **Why it is hard**<br>
  Single-trial EEG is noisy, and clinical recordings lose more trials
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 0:45 (cumulative 2:05). The task label in the data is "phonemes", but the stimuli are pure tones. We classify the condition of each trial (standard vs deviant), not the diagnostic group.
[Sources]
- LISTEN papers/Gatlinburg-2026.md: groups, paradigm, trial counts.
- Scott's clarification to the codex agent, 2026-10-01: stimuli are pure tones.
[/Sources]
:::

The abstract's N of 86 counted recordings. 87 decoded recordings come from 82 people; four of the five repeat participants are in the Angelman group, so AS shrinks from 14–15 recordings to 11 people. For the re-analysis we kept one session per person, chosen by most usable deviant trials before looking at any scores, and excluded sessions with fewer than 20 usable deviants or no usable data, leaving 78 people.

## Decoding In One Slide

::: {.decode-pipeline}
::: {.workflow-step}
**Single trials**<br>channels × time
:::
::: {.workflow-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.workflow-step}
**Classifier**<br>linear, regularized
:::
::: {.workflow-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.workflow-step}
**Cross-validation**<br>train ≠ test trials
:::
::: {.workflow-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.workflow-step}
**Score**<br>chance = 0.5
:::
:::

- One model per person; standard vs deviant at ~4 : 1
- Always guessing "standard": 80% accuracy, **50% balanced accuracy**

::: {.notes}
Timing: 0:45 (cumulative 3:50). Within each person we train a linear classifier on some trials and test it on held-out trials. Because standards outnumber deviants about four to one, plain accuracy is misleading: always guessing "standard" gets 80%. Balanced accuracy averages the recall of both classes, so that strategy scores 50%.
[Sources]
- LISTEN scripts/decode.py (original pipeline); codex evaluation slide (decoding-codex gatlinburg-2026/index.qmd).
[/Sources]
:::

## First Pass: Modestly Above 50%

![](figures/single-trial.png){.result-figure fig-alt="Participant-level single-trial balanced accuracy from the original pipeline. Means: TD 55.7%, verbal ASD 54.1%, minimally verbal ASD 53.4%, Angelman syndrome 56.9%."}

::: {.source-line}
Original pipeline (abstract): LDA on all channels × time. One dot per person (82 people); repeat sessions averaged.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 0:45 (cumulative 4:35). This is the abstract's analysis, re-summarized per person. Group means are 54–57%, with wide individual spread. Note that AS is the highest group, not the lowest, once sessions are weighted per person. The rest of the talk asks how far to trust these numbers.
[Sources]
- codex audit: artifacts/gatlinburg-2026/single_trial_participants.csv and group_summary.csv; figure from scripts/gatlinburg_figures.py (phonemes-decoding-2026-09-29).
[/Sources]

## 1. Pick An Imbalance-Aware Metric

::: {.image-text-slide}

::: {.image-panel}
![](figures/decoding/fig-metric.png){fig-alt="Per-participant scores for four scoring choices, with means: original balanced accuracy 0.550, logistic balanced accuracy 0.509, class-weighted logistic balanced accuracy 0.541, logistic AUC 0.566."}
:::

::: {.text-panel}
- Same model, same data:
  - balanced accuracy **0.51**
  - AUC **0.57**
- Classifier priors favour the majority class
- Report **AUC** (threshold-free), or weight the classes
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:00 (cumulative 5:35). Re-analysis pipeline: 100 Hz, 0–500 ms, L2 logistic regression, repeated 5×5-fold CV. Without class weighting the decision threshold favours standards, so balanced accuracy sits at 0.51 even though the scores separate the classes (AUC 0.57, paired Wilcoxon p < .001). Regularizing and downsampling the original model changed little (0.550 → 0.541 balanced accuracy); the metric choice matters more.
[Sources]
- LISTEN-claude results/decoding_v2/stats.md, section 1.
[/Sources]
:::

## 2. Averaging Needs A Trial Budget

![](figures/trial-budget.png){.result-figure fig-alt="Left: retained deviant trials per recording by group. Right: mean deviant pseudo-trials per test fold after five-trial averaging, about one to four."}

::: {.source-line}
Original pipeline: 5-trial averages built before cross-validation. One dot per recording.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:00 (cumulative 6:35). The abstract reported that averaging five trials helped TD and verbal ASD but not MV-ASD or AS. Look at the budget: after averaging, test folds hold one to four deviant averages, and fewest in the groups with fewest trials. With one deviant average in a fold, a single prediction moves deviant recall from 0 to 100%. That evaluation cannot tell us whether averaging helps.
[Sources]
- codex audit: artifacts/gatlinburg-2026/matched_sessions.csv; figure from scripts/gatlinburg_figures.py (phonemes-decoding-2026-09-29).
[/Sources]
:::

## 3. Average Inside The Folds

![](figures/decoding/fig-pseudo-compare.png){.result-figure fig-alt="Left: original pipeline balanced accuracy, single trial versus five-trial average built before cross-validation, by group. Right: AUC when averages are built inside the folds, rising with the number of trials averaged in every group."}

- Built inside train and test folds, averaging helps **every group**: 0.56 → 0.69 (k = 10)

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:15 (cumulative 7:50). Left, the original evaluation, same 78 people: averaging appears to help TD (0.557 → 0.594) and verbal ASD (0.541 → 0.572), barely MV-ASD (0.540 → 0.550), and to hurt AS (0.577 → 0.531). Note the two panels use different metrics. Right, averages built separately within training and test folds and repeated over random groupings: AUC rises with k in every group, including MV-ASD (0.54 → 0.66) and AS (0.59 → 0.73). Caveats: at k = 10 only 12 MV-ASD and 6 AS participants have enough trials, and this decodes averaged responses, not single trials.
[Sources]
- Left panel: LISTEN within_subject_decoding_results.csv and within_subject_decoding_results_pseudo.csv, restricted to the 78 analyzed sessions.
- Right panel: LISTEN-claude results/decoding_v2/stats.md, section 6. Figure: scripts/analyze_v2.py fig_pseudo_compare.
- Idea of overlaying the original pipeline: kimi draft (decoding-kimi, fig_pseudo).
[/Sources]
:::

## 4. Report Usable Trials

::: {.image-panel .fig-compact}
![](figures/decoding/fig-trials.png){fig-alt="Left: usable deviant trials per participant by group. Right: decoding AUC as a function of number of trials used, by group."}
:::

- MV-ASD and AS keep ~35% fewer deviants
- Fewer trials → lower AUC within person (TD, V-ASD)
- Here, group AUC did not differ, with or without trial count

::: {.notes}
Timing: 0:50 (cumulative 8:40). Median usable deviants: TD 94, V-ASD 84, MV-ASD 56, AS 58.5. Subsampling within person lowers AUC for TD and V-ASD. Across people, trial count did not predict AUC (Spearman rho 0.12), and the group effect was not significant with or without trial count as a covariate (p = .16 and .18; p = .08 when everyone is subsampled to 40 deviants). It did not drive our result, but it is a ready-made confound: check it and report it. Fewer participants contribute at higher trial counts in the right panel.
[Sources]
- LISTEN-claude results/decoding_v2/stats.md, section 5; results/decoding_v2/participants.csv.
[/Sources]
:::

## 5. Ask Who, Not Just How Many

::: {.image-panel .fig-compact}
![](figures/decoding/fig-individual.png){fig-alt="Left: AUC required for significance versus number of trials. Right: percentage of participants decoded above chance by group: TD 10 of 23, V-ASD 8 of 27, MV-ASD 4 of 18, AS 5 of 10."}
:::

- Chance is not 0.5: significance needs AUC 0.56–0.66
- Permutation tests: **35%** of individuals above chance

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:00 (cumulative 9:40). A group mean above 0.5 does not say which people can be decoded. With a 200-permutation test per person, 27 of 78 (35%) are above chance; all groups exceed the 5% expected by chance (binomial p ≤ .011). The threshold depends strongly on trial count: people with ~20 deviants need AUC around 0.65.
[Sources]
- LISTEN-claude results/decoding_v2/stats.md, section 3.
[/Sources]
:::

## Revised Results

::: {.results-table}

| | TD | V-ASD | MV-ASD | AS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Participants | 23 | 27 | 18 | 10 |
| Single-trial AUC | 0.57 | 0.57 | 0.54 | 0.59 |
| Above chance (group) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Individuals above chance | 10/23 | 8/27 | 4/18 | 5/10 |
| Pseudo-trial AUC (k = 5) | 0.63 | 0.64 | 0.60 | 0.66 |

:::

::: {.source-line}
Groups did not differ (p = .16). Decoding is also above chance *before* sound onset; see backup.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 0:50 (cumulative 10:30). Single-trial decoding is weak but above chance at the group level in every group (one-sided Wilcoxon, p ≤ .014). About a third of individuals pass their own test, and averaging inside the folds raises AUC everywhere. Groups did not differ significantly. One caveat, detailed in backup: the conditions are also decodable before the sound, and the ERP starts before 0 ms, which points to an event-timing or filtering problem to resolve before interpreting timing.
[Sources]
- LISTEN-claude results/decoding_v2/stats.md, sections 2, 3, 5, 6; baseline: results/decoding_v2/baseline_diagnostics.md.
[/Sources]
:::

## Recommendations

::: {.checklist}
- Define the prediction target: single trial, average, or new session
- Count **participants**, not recordings
- Use **AUC** (or class weights) with imbalanced designs
- Build averages **inside** CV folds; report the trial budget
- Test **individuals** with permutation nulls
- **Decode the baseline** as a sanity check
- Trace every number on a slide to a script
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1:00 (cumulative 11:30). Seven cheap checks; each one changed our interpretation of this dataset.
[Sources]
- Prediction target and unit of analysis: codex draft, Varoquaux et al. 2017.
- Claim-to-source ledger: kimi and codex drafts.
- Remaining items: LISTEN-claude results/decoding_v2/stats.md and baseline_diagnostics.md.
[/Sources]
:::

## Limitations & Next Steps

- Verify event timing against sound onset (backup)
- Noise or more variable responses in MV-ASD / AS?
- Test–retest across repeat sessions
- Link decoding to language scores (planned)

::: {.notes}
Timing: 0:45 (cumulative 12:15). First, check the event timing: decoding and the ERP both start before 0 ms. Then ask whether lower decodability in some participants reflects noise or more variable auditory processing; repeat sessions give a first test–retest check. Associations with language scores are planned and not analyzed here.
[Sources]

# Backup

## Decoding Before The Sound {#backup-baseline}

::: {.image-text-slide}

::: {.image-panel}
![](figures/decoding/fig-baseline.png){fig-alt="Group-mean time-resolved decoding AUC from −200 to 500 ms; AUC is above chance before sound onset."}
:::

::: {.text-panel}
- AUC = **0.55** before onset (p < .001)
- Shuffled labels: 0.50
- Not carry-over, sequence position, or drift
- Candidate causes:
  - markers offset from sound onset
  - 1 Hz high-pass + baseline correction
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Backup. The conditions are decodable before the sound (mean pre-stimulus AUC 0.549, p < .001; 53 of 78 participants peak before onset). Ruled out on 8 participants: classifier bias (label-shuffle null 0.501 ± 0.010), previous-trial carry-over, run-length position, drift, and epoch-filter smearing. Two candidates remain: event markers placed after the true sound onset, or a 1 Hz high-pass on continuous data followed by baseline correction (van Driel, Olivers & Fahrenfort, 2021). The events files have no audio-onset channel, so this could not be checked.
[Sources]
- LISTEN-claude results/decoding_v2/stats.md, section 4; results/decoding_v2/baseline_diagnostics.md.
[/Sources]
:::

## Time Course And ERP By Group {#backup-time-course}

![](figures/decoding/fig-time-resolved.png){.result-figure fig-alt="Time-resolved decoding AUC (top) and deviant-minus-standard ERP (bottom) for each group."}

::: {.source-line}
Bars: clusters above chance (one-sided cluster permutation). In MV-ASD and AS, significant clusters are only before onset. The difference wave turns negative near −100 ms.
:::

::: {.notes}
Backup. The grand-average ERP shows no clear N1 after onset, and the deviant negativity begins around −100 ms. A sharp onset like this is more typical of a timing offset than a filter smear. If the markers are offset, the fixed MMN windows used in the notebooks (100–300 ms) are misplaced too.
[Sources]
- LISTEN-claude results/decoding_v2/stats.md, section 4; results/decoding_v2/baseline_diagnostics.md, "Grand-average ERP timing".
[/Sources]
:::

## Analysis Details {#backup-methods}

::: {.methods-table}

| Component | Re-analysis |
|:--|:--|
| Epochs | −200–500 ms; 150 µV rejection; average reference |
| Features | 0–500 ms in 10 ms bins (100 Hz), all channels |
| Model | Scaler + L2 logistic, class-weighted (C = 0.001; per-bin C = 1) |
| Evaluation | Repeated 5 × 5-fold CV; AUC and balanced accuracy |
| Individuals | 200-permutation test per participant |
| Averaging | Pseudo-trials within train and test folds, k = 1–10 |
| Sample | One session per person; ≥ 20 usable deviants |

:::

::: {.notes}
Backup. The pipeline was fixed in advance from an 8-participant pilot; no tuning. The original pipeline used all 701 samples at 1 kHz with unregularized LDA and single 5-fold CV.
[Sources]
- LISTEN-claude scripts/decode_v2.py and scripts/analyze_v2.py.
[/Sources]
:::
